outputs.L3:
The method creates a protective sealing layer within a landfill basin intended for industrial and mining slurries. A single-ply or multi-ply base sealing layer is first installed across the basin floor and over the surrounding embankment ring up to the basin’s maximum filling level.

Water-permeable, multi-ply geotextile protective mats are then placed over the base sealing layer. These mats incorporate separate flexible tubes formed between parallel connecting lines. On the basin floor, the protective tube mats are laid across the bottom area. Along the embankment, the mats are arranged so that their tubes extend in the direction of the slope or at an acute angle to it.

Each flexible tube is filled individually with an aqueous suspension. Once a tube has been filled to the required level, its filling opening is sealed, thereby forming a continuous protective layer over the underlying base seal.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for producing a protective sealing layer in a landfill basin intended to receive industrial or mining slurries. The basin includes a substantially horizontal bottom and surrounding sloped embankment surfaces, both of which are provided with a base sealing layer. To protect this base sealing layer against mechanical damage, erosion, displacement, and other stresses arising during filling and operation of the basin, water-permeable, multi-ply geotextile tube mats are installed over the sealed surfaces.

Each geotextile mat comprises a plurality of separate, elongated tubes formed between connected layers of water-permeable geotextile material. The mats are laid over the bottom of the basin and extended onto the embankment up to at least the intended maximum filling level. On the sloped embankment surfaces, the tubes are oriented substantially in the direction of the slope. This alignment allows the filled tubes to conform to the embankment geometry and improves the stability and continuity of the protective covering.

After the mats have been positioned, the individual tubes are filled with an aqueous suspension. Water contained in the suspension can pass through the permeable geotextile, while the suspended solid material is retained within the tubes. As dewatering proceeds, the retained solids form a stable filling that gives each tube its protective shape and mechanical resistance. The tubes are filled separately so that the amount of filling can be adapted to local conditions, including changes in slope, surface irregularities, and differing protection requirements across the basin.

Once a tube has received the required quantity of suspension, it is sealed to prevent the retained material from escaping. The process is repeated for the remaining tubes until the desired portions of the basin bottom and embankment are covered by a continuous arrangement of filled and sealed tube mats. Adjacent mats may be positioned so that gaps in the protective layer are avoided and the underlying base seal remains covered throughout the relevant area.

The completed mat system forms an adaptable protective layer over both horizontal and inclined surfaces. It distributes loads, shields the base sealing layer from direct contact with deposited slurry, and reduces the risk of puncture or abrasion during basin filling. Because the multi-ply mats can follow variations in the basin profile and the tubes can be filled individually, the system provides secure coverage from the bottom of the basin upward along the embankment to the maximum filling level.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest yet most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it identifies a particular person, place, object, or idea. Saying “the book,” for example, points to a specific book rather than just any book.

Although simple, “the” brings clarity and precision to communication. It helps readers understand what is already known, unique, or especially important in a sentence. This tiny word demonstrates how even the most ordinary parts of language can play an essential role in expressing meaning.

counterfactuals.output:
## Title

**Geotextile Tube-Mat System for Lined Slurry Containment Basins**

## Abstract

A liner-protection and ballast system is provided for installation over a base liner of an industrial or mining slurry containment basin. The system includes a geotextile mat positioned above a single-ply or multi-ply base liner and a plurality of elongate geotextile tubes coupled to or integrally formed with the mat. The tubes are configured to receive a pumpable fill material and, when filled, define spaced ballast members that restrain the mat against the base liner. The mat distributes loads, limits direct contact between settled solids and the base liner, and provides a recoverable interface during removal of deposited slurry solids. Fluid-transmissive regions between or through the tubes permit migration of liquid while reducing uplift, wrinkling, erosion, and mechanical damage to the base liner. The system may include sacrificial wear layers, drainage layers, leak-detection layers, filtration regions, anchoring components, and tube filling and drainage fittings. Methods of installing, filling, operating, and recovering the tube-mat system are also disclosed.

## Technical Field

The disclosure relates to lined containment structures and, more particularly, to geosynthetic protection, ballast, drainage, and solids-management systems installed over single-ply or multi-ply base liners in industrial process-water, tailings, sludge, ash, brine, sediment, and mining slurry containment basins.

## Background

Industrial and mining slurry containment basins commonly employ geomembrane liners to limit seepage into underlying soil and groundwater. A base lining system may include one or more polymeric geomembranes, geosynthetic clay liners, compacted clay layers, geotextile cushions, drainage geocomposites, and leak-detection layers.

During placement, settling, consolidation, and removal of slurry solids, the base liner may be subjected to puncture, abrasion, tensile strain, localized bearing loads, hydraulic uplift, wrinkling, drag forces, and damage from excavation or solids-recovery equipment. Conventional cover soils or aggregate ballast can be difficult to place without damaging the liner and may contaminate the contained material or interfere with recovery operations.

Accordingly, a need exists for a deployable geosynthetic system that protects and stabilizes the base liner, accommodates basin geometry and liner movement, permits controlled liquid migration, and provides a detectable or recoverable boundary above which deposited solids may be removed.

## Summary of the Disclosure

In one aspect, a containment system includes:

1. a basin subgrade;
2. a base liner supported by the subgrade, the base liner comprising at least one fluid-impermeable geomembrane;
3. a geotextile mat extending over at least a portion of the base liner; and
4. a plurality of elongate geotextile tubes disposed on, attached to, or integrally formed with the geotextile mat.

Each tube defines an internal chamber configured to receive pumpable fill material. Filled tubes provide distributed ballast while the mat provides liner protection and load distribution. The tubes may be arranged in parallel, intersecting, serpentine, cellular, radial, circumferential, or contour-following patterns.

The tube-mat system may be deployed as prefabricated panels. Adjacent panels may be joined by sewing, lacing, zippers, mechanical connectors, thermal welding, adhesive bonding, overlap flaps, or combinations thereof. The system may be anchored at a basin crest, perimeter trench, intermediate bench, sump, or other structural feature.

The fill material may include water, process liquid, clarified supernatant, slurry, tailings, sand slurry, fine aggregate, cementitious material, polymer-enhanced material, or combinations thereof. Fill material may be introduced after placement of the unfilled system so that the system can be installed with limited point loading on the base liner.

## Detailed Description

### Base Liner Assembly

The base liner may be a single-ply liner including one geomembrane, or a multi-ply liner including first and second geomembranes separated by a drainage or leak-detection layer. Suitable geomembranes include high-density polyethylene, linear low-density polyethylene, flexible polypropylene, polyvinyl chloride, ethylene propylene diene monomer, bituminous geomembranes, and combinations thereof.

A cushioning geotextile or geocomposite may be positioned between the base liner and the tube-mat system. In multi-ply embodiments, the tube-mat system may be hydraulically isolated from an inter-liner leak-detection space.

### Geotextile Mat

The mat may include woven, nonwoven, knitted, composite, coated, or laminated geotextile material. The mat may be permeable to liquid while retaining slurry solids having a selected particle-size distribution. Alternatively, selected portions of the mat may be coated or laminated to provide reduced permeability.

The mat may include:

- a lower cushioning layer facing the base liner;
- an upper wear or sacrificial layer facing the basin interior;
- a reinforcement scrim;
- a filtration layer;
- a drainage layer;
- high-visibility or contrasting indicia indicating proximity to the base liner;
- electrically conductive or detectable elements for locating the mat; and
- embedded strain, pressure, moisture, or leak-detection sensors.

The lower surface may be substantially free of rigid projections. Seams, ports, and connectors may be positioned or padded to avoid concentrated loading of the base liner.

### Geotextile Tubes

Each tube may be formed by joining an upper geotextile sheet to the mat along spaced longitudinal seams. Alternatively, a separately manufactured tube may be connected to the mat by stitching, welding, lacing, bonding, or mechanical attachment.

The tubes may have circular, oval, flattened, lobed, or multi-cell cross sections. Internal ties, webs, baffles, or partitions may control tube height and limit rolling. A tube may have a filled height selected to create a predetermined clearance or excavation-control elevation above the base liner.

Tube spacing may define exposed or covered drainage corridors. Interconnecting conduits may hydraulically connect selected tubes to permit common filling, pressure equalization, drainage, or sequential filling. Valves may isolate individual tubes or groups of tubes.

Fill ports may be located above an anticipated slurry elevation, at a perimeter manifold, or within accessible service chambers. Pressure-relief devices may limit internal tube pressure. Drain ports may permit removal, reuse, repositioning, or controlled collapse of the tubes.

### Hydraulic and Mechanical Functions

The filled tubes apply ballast to resist flotation and displacement of the mat. The mat distributes localized forces over a larger liner area and reduces abrasion caused by relative movement between deposited solids and the base liner.

Liquid may migrate:

- through permeable portions of the mat;
- through channels formed between adjacent tubes;
- through an integrated drainage core;
- toward a sump or decant structure; or
- through controlled openings fitted with geotextile filters.

Tube orientation may be selected to direct drainage toward a collection sump while resisting downslope migration of settled solids. On basin side slopes, the tubes may extend generally along contours, generally downslope, or in an intersecting grid.

The tube-mat system may function as a physical and visual excavation limit. During removal of settled slurry solids, the tubes may provide tactile resistance and stand-off distance that reduce the likelihood that excavation equipment contacts the base liner.

### Panelized Construction

The system may include modular panels sized for transport and deployment. Each panel may include one or more tubes and peripheral connection regions. Adjacent panels may overlap in a shingled arrangement oriented relative to the expected direction of slurry flow or solids-removal operations.

Expansion regions, folds, pleats, or extensible connectors may accommodate differential settlement and thermal movement. Breakaway or selectively releasable connections may prevent excessive loads from being transferred to the base liner or perimeter anchorage.

### Installation Method

An installation method may include:

1. preparing the basin subgrade;
2. installing a single-ply or multi-ply base liner;
3. inspecting and testing the base liner;
4. deploying the tube-mat system in an unfilled or partially filled condition;
5. joining adjacent panels;
6. anchoring selected portions without penetrating the fluid-containment portion of the base liner;
7. introducing fill material into the tubes at a controlled flow rate and pressure;
8. monitoring tube height, pressure, and liner condition; and
9. introducing slurry into the basin after the tubes achieve a selected ballast condition.

Filling may proceed from a low point toward a high point, from the perimeter inward, or in alternating tube groups to limit wrinkling or displacement of the base liner.

## Exemplary Claims

### Independent System Claim

1. **A lined slurry containment system comprising:**

   a basin having a floor and at least one side slope;

   a base liner supported by the basin, the base liner comprising at least one geomembrane configured to restrict migration of liquid from the basin;

   a geotextile mat disposed above and extending across at least a portion of the base liner; and

   a plurality of elongate geotextile tubes coupled to the geotextile mat, each geotextile tube defining an internal chamber configured to receive a pumpable fill material,

   wherein the geotextile tubes, when containing the pumpable fill material, form spaced ballast members that retain the geotextile mat relative to the base liner, and

   wherein at least one fluid-transmissive region is defined through the geotextile mat or between adjacent ones of the geotextile tubes.

2. The system of claim 1, wherein the base liner comprises a first geomembrane, a second geomembrane, and a leak-detection layer positioned between the first and second geomembranes.

3. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile mat comprises a lower cushioning layer and an upper sacrificial wear layer.

4. The system of claim 1, wherein at least one of the geotextile tubes is integrally formed by joining an upper geotextile sheet to the geotextile mat along spaced seams.

5. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile tubes include internal ties that limit a filled height of the geotextile tubes.

6. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile tubes are arranged in a grid defining a plurality of fluid-flow corridors.

7. The system of claim 1, wherein at least a subset of the geotextile tubes extends along a contour of the side slope to resist downslope movement of deposited slurry solids.

8. The system of claim 1, further comprising a manifold in fluid communication with a plurality of the geotextile tubes and configured to selectively fill or drain the plurality of geotextile tubes.

9. The system of claim 1, wherein the pumpable fill material comprises at least one of water, process liquid, slurry, tailings, sand slurry, fine aggregate, or cementitious material.

10. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile mat has an apparent opening size selected to permit passage of liquid while retaining at least a portion of solids contained in a slurry received by the basin.

11. The system of claim 1, further comprising a drainage geocomposite positioned between the geotextile mat and the base liner.

12. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile mat includes a visually detectable layer having a color contrasting with deposited slurry solids.

13. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile mat includes at least one sensor configured to detect strain, pressure, moisture, temperature, or electrical leakage.

14. The system of claim 1, wherein lower surfaces of the geotextile mat and the geotextile tubes are substantially free of rigid projections capable of puncturing the base liner.

15. The system of claim 1, wherein the geotextile mat and the geotextile tubes collectively define a removable excavation-control layer positioned above the base liner.

### Independent Tube-Mat Article Claim

16. **A geotextile tube-mat assembly for placement over a geomembrane liner, the assembly comprising:**

   a flexible geotextile panel having an upper surface, a lower liner-facing surface, and first and second peripheral connection regions;

   a plurality of inflatable elongate chambers supported by the flexible geotextile panel;

   at least one fill fitting in fluid communication with the plurality of inflatable elongate chambers; and

   a plurality of liquid-flow paths extending between the inflatable elongate chambers,

   wherein the inflatable elongate chambers are fillable after deployment of the flexible geotextile panel over the geomembrane liner to provide distributed ballast without placement of loose aggregate directly on the geomembrane liner.

17. The assembly of claim 16, wherein the first and second peripheral connection regions are configured to connect the flexible geotextile panel to respective adjacent geotextile panels.

18. The assembly of claim 16, further comprising a pressure-relief device configured to limit pressure within at least one of the inflatable elongate chambers.

19. The assembly of claim 16, wherein the lower liner-facing surface comprises a nonwoven cushioning geotextile.

20. The assembly of claim 16, further comprising an expansion region configured to accommodate differential settlement of the geomembrane liner.

### Independent Method Claim

21. **A method of protecting a base liner in a slurry containment basin, the method comprising:**

   installing a base liner over at least a portion of the slurry containment basin;

   deploying a flexible geotextile mat over the base liner while a plurality of geotextile tubes coupled to the flexible geotextile mat are in an unfilled or partially filled condition;

   introducing pumpable fill material into the plurality of geotextile tubes to form distributed ballast members above the base liner;

   introducing a slurry into the slurry containment basin such that solids from the slurry accumulate above the flexible geotextile mat; and

   transmitting liquid from the slurry through or along at least one fluid-flow path associated with the flexible geotextile mat.

22. The method of claim 21, further comprising controlling a filling sequence or filling pressure of the geotextile tubes to limit wrinkling of the base liner.

23. The method of claim 21, further comprising removing accumulated solids to an elevation defined by upper portions of the filled geotextile tubes while maintaining separation between solids-removal equipment and the base liner.

24. The method of claim 21, further comprising draining at least a portion of the pumpable fill material and removing or repositioning the flexible geotextile mat.

25. The method of claim 21, wherein installing the base liner comprises installing first and second geomembranes with a leak-detection layer therebetween, and wherein deploying the flexible geotextile mat is performed without penetrating either geomembrane within a fluid-containment area of the basin.
